topic.title: Trailer view counts are a marketing budget
topic.claim: 'Most viewed trailer in 24 hours' tells you how much was spent promoting it, not how much people want to watch the film.
topic.moment: A poster announces a trailer record, and fans fight in comments over whose star won.

turn.actually: Views come from ads, pushes and fan clubs, and the record is announced to create more hype.

topic.because: A big number makes undecided viewers feel they're missing something. The record is part of the marketing, not a result of it.
topic.payoff: Watch the films that broke trailer records and check how many actually ran in theatres.
topic.behaviour: Studios promote trailers heavily and post 'record' numbers within a day.
topic.mechanism: A big number creates the hype it claims to measure.
topic.group: Film fans who track box office talk
topic.send_to: The friend who fights star fan wars over trailer views.
topic.why_now: Big releases are lining up for the year-end and holiday window.
topic.needs_facts: Whether paid ad plays count toward public YouTube view numbers.

score.why: A trailer record is part of the marketing, not a result of it. Fan wars are the obvious audience.

topic.villain: a trailer-record PR tactic designed to manufacture hype it then measures
